entries.title: ibm
entries.html:
i came across ibm's hat, while stumbling my way around the artificial intelligence ring where all the big tech companies have been forced to throw theirs.

that is to say that i like what they've got to offer. the granite-4 models are state-of-the-art, they're small, which seems to be the trend lately, and make bold an i'm sure substantiated claims of beating much larger models of the previous generation (which most of their competitors are still offering as their flagship products, so good on them for being the quickest out of the gate.)

it's a 4B or 7B parameter model, and what's more, it's not a transformer like almost all of the competitors and the biggest names in the space. i hadn't realized this at first, but the mamba models are actually a completely different architecture, sharing very little except the most basic of components, and of course the autograd system that allows for gradient descent on large differentiable systems by incremental computations serially at each layer, which is what has really fanned the flames of the whole AI apocalypse. i wonder if the pythonistas that dreamed that up are proud of what they've done? j/k, i'm sure they are. that's a bob moog reference. go see the film biography if you aren't familiar, it'll have you in tears towards the end. what a beautiful person, and a truly brilliant engineer. bob moog was someone who could understand machines and circuits on so many levels, including deeply personal and even spiritual.

another part of their panoplie that i find particularly interesting is their docling project, which claims to be a comprehensive and major advancement in visual document understanding systems. read as: ocr for documents that actually works, even for things with columns, tables, and (and this is the really impressive part) even graphs, charts and equations. it can ingest pretty much anything, which it renders to high resolution images before processing with a combination (think MoE) of VLMs, that are trained to conditionally produce markdown, HTML, LaTeX and plaintext, and can extract images of anything it can't represent with the selected output format, outputting references and placeholders or inline base64 encoded data:// URLs.

I'm planning on testing it out on the DTIC archive, which I started scraping a year or two ago, with the intent of turning it into a dataset of advanced research materials and military industrial complex lingo. I feel like a model trained on that might be of use to plenty of people, but the problem I ran into was that most of the files were scanned from ancient three ring binders of hand typed (in some cases) reports, and I did not have a great solution at the time for converting them into high-enough quality text to make building a dataset possible. 

Problem solved?

I hope so. I guess we shall see shortly.
